extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, and researchers interested in Stephenie Meyer / the Twilight series
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style author biography and critical reception summary describing Stephenie Meyer's life, religious influences, stylistic choices, controversies (feminism, depictions of relationships), adaptations, awards, and bibliography. Not an instruction manual but contains descriptive statements that imply creative-writing choices and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid graphic sexual content
rubrics_metrics.description: "Despite pressure to include a major sex scene, Meyer was adamant against including graphic sex in her series."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes Meyer resisted adding explicit sex, and critics/observers (e.g., Lev Grossman of Time) attribute part of the series' appeal to its lack of sex and its eroticizing of abstinence. Use of explicit sexual scenes is presented as a deliberate authorial choice; one exception in Meyer's work is The Host (2008), which contains drinking and more adult content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude drinking and smoking in characters
rubrics_metrics.description: "She does not drink alcohol or coffee, smoke... Similarly, there is no drinking and smoking in the novels (with the exception of her 2008 The Host, which contains drinking)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of substance use in characters aligns with the author's personal practices and is presented as a consistent element of her novels (except The Host). For writers aiming for similar tone/audience expectations, minimizing depiction of drinking/smoking reinforces a 'clean' or family-friendly image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write characters who contemplate origins and destiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Meyer says her characters "tend to think more about where they came from and where they are going, than might be typical."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize introspection about past and future in characterization. This reflective orientation contributes to thematic depth and can be a recurring motif across characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep tone light; avoid graphic/dark content
rubrics_metrics.description: Meyer: "I don't think my books are going to be really graphic or dark, because of who I am. There's always going to be a lot of light in my stories."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an overall lighter, less graphic tone when aiming for the emotional register associated with Meyer's work. Darkness/graphic depictions are intentionally minimized and therefore may clash with audience expectations tied to this style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use titles to symbolically reinforce thematic arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: "The titles of the novels serve to reinforce this idea... Twilight, New Moon, and Eclipse serve as natural phenomenon in which the sun is darkened. However, the final novel is titled Breaking Dawn, which symbolizes the beginning of a new day and Bella's transformation..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select book/section titles that function as symbolic markers of theme and character transformation (e.g., natural phenomena mirroring narrative or emotional states). Titles can be structured to map a progression (darkening → renewal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Center the narrative on the protagonist's choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Meyer has dismissed criticism by saying the books "center around Bella's choice" and that the heroine's 'damsel in distress' persona is due only to her humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame pivotal plot events and moral/relationship decisions as the protagonist's choices to foreground agency. Even when protagonists appear passive, emphasize the presence of deliberation/choice to counter readings that portray them as lacking autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid romanticizing abusive dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue the series "romanticizes a physically abusive relationship," citing Bella's life revolving around Edward, lack of control, absolute dependence on his protection, and physical injuries from consummation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records sustained criticism that portraying a protagonist as utterly dependent or as centering their entire life on a partner can be read as endorsing unhealthy/abusive dynamics. As a guideline or anti-pattern, be cautious about depicting dependency as idealized or without consequences; ensure relationships include consent, agency, and critical context if they depict imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray feminism as the ability to choose
rubrics_metrics.description: Meyer: her definition of feminism is "the ability for a woman to choose, and the definition of anti-feminism is removing the choice... from the woman entirely."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If engaging feminist themes, depict women's choices (including traditional roles such as staying home or having children) as valid options rather than automatically problematic. Be aware that different readers/scholars may interpret such portrayals variably—some label them traditional rather than feminist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow an author's faith/values to subtly shape thematic content
rubrics_metrics.description: Meyer, a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, acknowledges her faith has influenced her work; she cites reading the Book of Mormon as having 'the most significant impact on [her] life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious or personal values may manifest indirectly through recurring motifs (e.g., abstinence, spiritual purity, contemplation of destiny). Authors choosing to incorporate their beliefs should expect that readers and scholars may read those influences into themes and character behavior, and it may affect reception in cultural critique.
